article_title: Buying vs Leasing a Car in India — The Math Most People Get Wrong
claim: A 5-year loan at roughly 9% interest, after a 20% down payment on a ₹10 lakh car, runs an EMI around ₹16,600/month
source: Standard EMI amortization formula applied to an ₹8,00,000 principal at 9% p.a. over 60 months; rate range cross-checked against BankBazaar's published car loan interest rates
required_correction: Math checks out: EMI computes to ~₹16,603/month, and 9% falls within the currently advertised 7.45%-10% range. No numeric correction needed, but the article should disclose it's an illustrative rate since actual rates vary 250+ bps by lender and credit profile.

article_title: Buying vs Leasing a Car in India — The Math Most People Get Wrong
claim: Total repayment on the 5-year loan runs around ₹9.96 lakh on top of the ₹2 lakh down payment
source: Standard EMI amortization formula (₹16,603/month × 60 months ≈ ₹9,96,180)
required_correction: Consistent with the EMI figure above; no correction needed.

article_title: Buying vs Leasing a Car in India — The Math Most People Get Wrong
claim: After 5 years of loan ownership, the car is worth perhaps ₹4-5 lakh in resale value (on a ₹10 lakh car)
source: IRDAI standard IDV depreciation schedule (insurance valuation table by vehicle age)
required_correction: IRDAI's depreciation table puts a 5-year-old car's IDV at roughly 50% of original ex-showroom price (~₹5 lakh on a ₹10 lakh car), consistent with the article's range, but that is an insurance-valuation figure, not actual market resale price, which often runs lower. Article should clarify this is a rough estimate, not sourced to an official figure, and that real resale depends heavily on brand/model/condition.

article_title: Buying vs Leasing a Car in India — The Math Most People Get Wrong
claim: A comparable 3-year lease on the same ₹10 lakh car might run ₹18,000-22,000/month with no down payment, totaling ₹6.5-8 lakh over 3 years
required_correction: No named Indian leasing company (Orix, ALD Automotive, Mahindra) or published rate card was found backing this specific range for a ₹10 lakh vehicle. The article presents an invented 'comparable' figure as if benchmarked against real quotes. Should either cite an actual lessor's published rate or clearly flag the range as an illustrative estimate.

article_title: Buying vs Leasing a Car in India — The Math Most People Get Wrong
claim: Leases commonly cap annual mileage (often 10,000-15,000 km/year) with real per-km penalties beyond that, commonly ₹5-10 per km
source: Orix India retail leasing terms; general Indian car-leasing market summaries
required_correction: Indian lease providers, including Orix (the market's largest player), typically advertise mileage caps closer to 15,000-20,000 km/year, with per-km overage penalties more commonly in the ₹8-18/km range — both meaningfully higher than the article's stated 10,000-15,000 km cap and ₹5-10/km penalty. Both figures should be revised upward, and a specific lessor's published terms should be cited.

article_title: Buying vs Leasing a Car in India — The Math Most People Get Wrong
claim: Used car loan rates in India typically run 2 to 4 percentage points higher than new car loan rates
source: Forbes Advisor India car loan interest rate guide; BankBazaar used car loan rates
required_correction: Aggregated data shows new car loans averaging roughly 8% and used car loans roughly 9.45-10%+, a typical gap closer to 1.5-2 percentage points, widening toward 4 points only for older vehicles or weaker credit profiles. The article's '2 to 4' range is defensible but skews toward the high end for a typical borrower; consider narrowing to '1.5 to 4 points depending on the vehicle's age and your credit profile.'

article_title: Buying vs Leasing a Car in India — The Math Most People Get Wrong
claim: New cars lose a disproportionate share of their value in the first year, often 15-20%
source: IRDAI IDV Depreciation Table (official insurance valuation schedule); Cars24/Coverfox market depreciation analyses
required_correction: IRDAI's official schedule shows 15% depreciation by the 1-year mark, matching the low end of the article's claim, but independent market surveys (Cars24, Coverfox) commonly cite real-world first-year depreciation closer to 20-30%. The article's 15-20% range is on the conservative/low side; consider widening to roughly 15-25%.

article_title: Buying vs Leasing a Car in India — The Math Most People Get Wrong
claim: You run a business and can claim the lease as a deductible expense — this is the strongest, most common legitimate case for leasing in India
required_correction: The underlying tax mechanic (lease rentals are deductible business expenses, unlike loan EMIs, where only interest and depreciation are deductible) is real, but ranking it as the 'strongest, most common' reason is an editorial judgment, not a sourced statistic. Should be flagged as informed opinion rather than presented as settled fact.

article_title: How Your Bank Sends an OTP in Under Two Seconds
claim: Regulatory changes enforced by TRAI require every business sender, including banks, to register its SMS templates and sender IDs on a Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) platform before telecom operators will deliver the message at all
source: TRAI — Telecom Commercial Communications Customer Preference Regulations (TCCCPR), 2018
required_correction: Core claim is accurate — TCCCPR 2018 mandates DLT registration of Principal Entities, telemarketers, sender headers, and content templates, later reinforced by a February 2025 amendment. Article should name 'TCCCPR, 2018' (and the 2025 amendment) explicitly instead of the vague 'regulatory changes enforced by TRAI' — this is exactly the missing-citation gap flagged editorially.

article_title: How Your Bank Sends an OTP in Under Two Seconds
claim: OTPs travel through a separate 'transactional SMS route' that is exempt from many of the throttling rules applied to promotional traffic
source: TCCCPR 2018 — Promotional (P) vs Service/Transactional (S/T) SMS header classification and associated exemptions
required_correction: Accurate — transactional/service messages are exempt from the DND time-window restrictions that apply to promotional messages (e.g., an OTP can be sent at 2am, a promo cannot). Article should cite this classification by its regulatory name rather than describing it generically.

article_title: How Your Bank Sends an OTP in Under Two Seconds
claim: DND settings can sometimes interfere with delivery, though transactional OTPs are generally exempted
source: TCCCPR 2018 DND/time-restriction exemption for transactional messages
required_correction: Consistent with TRAI's framework. No numeric correction needed beyond adding the citation to TCCCPR 2018.

article_title: How Your Bank Sends an OTP in Under Two Seconds
claim: Bank OTP messages typically travel over SMPP (Short Message Peer-to-Peer), a direct persistent connection between the bank's SMS gateway provider and the telecom operator's SMS center
source: Industry SMS gateway documentation describing SMPP as the standard protocol for enterprise/bank bulk-transactional SMS delivery in India
required_correction: Technically accurate description of standard enterprise SMS gateway architecture, though the article cites no source. Recommend citing an SMS gateway/telecom technical reference (e.g., Infobip, Exotel documentation).

article_title: How Your Bank Sends an OTP in Under Two Seconds
claim: Some OTPs are delivered over the traditional 2G/3G signaling channel rather than the data connection, so a phone with poor basic signal but working data can still miss an OTP
source: General GSM/SS7 SMS delivery architecture — SMS rides the cellular signaling plane, independent of a data session
required_correction: Directionally correct, but the '2G/3G' framing oversimplifies: SMS has always used the signaling plane rather than the data/IP plane, and this persists on 4G (via CS fallback or SMS-over-IMS) too, not just legacy networks. Reword to 'cellular signaling channel' generally so readers on 4G/5G phones don't assume they're unaffected.

article_title: How Your Bank Sends an OTP in Under Two Seconds
claim: A growing number of banks are shifting critical OTP delivery to in-app push notifications routed through Firebase Cloud Messaging or Apple's Push Notification service
required_correction: Directionally plausible (push-based transaction approval is a known fintech trend) but no specific Indian bank, product, or source was found substantiating this as a current widespread shift. Should either name real examples or soften to a general industry-trend statement rather than an unqualified 'growing number' claim.

article_title: How Your Bank Sends an OTP in Under Two Seconds
claim: Reading an OTP aloud to a caller claiming to be from your bank is one of the most common fraud patterns in India specifically
required_correction: The underlying advice (never share an OTP) is standard, correct RBI/bank guidance. The specific prevalence claim ('one of the most common fraud patterns in India specifically') is not backed by a cited statistic and no specific RBI/CERT-In figure was located during this research pass. Recommend citing RBI or CERT-In published fraud data if available, or softening the superlative.

article_title: Google Sheets vs Excel — Which One Fits How You Work
claim: Excel requires a Microsoft 365 subscription for full functionality, though a limited free web version exists — presented without a specific INR figure despite cost being framed as a deciding factor
source: Microsoft 365 official India pricing page
required_correction: This is the exact gap flagged editorially. Current official India pricing: Microsoft 365 Personal ₹689/month (₹6,899/year); Microsoft 365 Family ₹819/month (₹8,199/year, up to 6 people). Article should state these actual INR figures instead of leaving the cost comparison abstract.

article_title: Google Sheets vs Excel — Which One Fits How You Work
claim: Google Sheets caps out around 10 million cells per spreadsheet
source: Google Drive Help — file size and storage limits
required_correction: Accurate — Google's current official limit is 10 million cells (or 18,278 columns) per spreadsheet. No correction needed.

article_title: Google Sheets vs Excel — Which One Fits How You Work
claim: Excel's row ceiling is over a million rows per sheet
source: Microsoft Office support — Excel specifications and limits
required_correction: Accurate — Excel's per-sheet row limit is exactly 1,048,576 rows (2^20), consistent with 'over a million.' Consider stating the exact figure for precision.

article_title: Google Sheets vs Excel — Which One Fits How You Work
claim: Sheets uses Apps Script, which can trigger on a schedule, on form submission, or on an email arriving, without your computer being on
source: Google Apps Script official documentation — installable triggers
required_correction: Accurate description of Apps Script's time-driven, form-submit, and other installable server-side triggers. No correction needed.

article_title: Google Sheets vs Excel — Which One Fits How You Work
claim: Excel's Power Query and Power Pivot handle serious data-modeling and multi-table joins better than anything native to Sheets
required_correction: Power Query/Power Pivot are real Excel features that outperform Sheets natively for large relational data modeling, but 'better than anything native to Sheets' is a comparative value judgment rather than a discrete checkable fact; label as informed opinion.

article_title: Notion vs Google Docs — What Each One Is Actually Built For
claim: Notion's free tier is generous for individuals but has real limits for teams — block count, file upload size, guest count — stated without any actual numbers
source: Notion official pricing page
required_correction: This is the flagged pricing gap. Current Notion free plan: unlimited blocks/pages for a single-member workspace but a block-count cap once multiple members join; individual file uploads capped at 5MB (uncapped on paid plans); up to 10 guests; 7-day page history (vs. 30 days on Plus at $10/member/month, 90 days on Business at $20/member/month). Article should state these concrete figures and the Plus-tier price for a proper cost comparison.

article_title: Notion vs Google Docs — What Each One Is Actually Built For
claim: Google Docs is effectively free with any Google account, bundled with the rest of Workspace
source: Google Workspace / Google Docs general product documentation
required_correction: Accurate for personal/free Google accounts, but the 'bundled with the rest of Workspace' phrasing glosses over that Google Workspace itself is a paid product for organizations — worth clarifying that Docs is free only in the free personal-account context, not that Workspace overall is free.

article_title: Notion vs Google Docs — What Each One Is Actually Built For
claim: Notion's offline support is more limited and has historically been less consistent, particularly for complex database views
source: Notion Help Center — offline mode documentation
required_correction: Directionally accurate — Notion's offline mode requires pages to have been recently opened/cached, and complex database views can fail to sync offline, per Notion's own documentation. Article's characterization is fair but should cite Notion's help docs directly rather than presenting it as general knowledge.

article_title: Notion vs Google Docs — What Each One Is Actually Built For
claim: Google Docs' offline mode is mature and reliable once enabled, usable for writing on a flight or in an area with patchy connectivity
source: Google Docs Editors Help — offline access documentation
required_correction: Accurate — Google Docs offline mode, once enabled via the Chrome extension/browser setting, is well-documented and reliable for basic editing without connectivity. No correction needed.

article_title: How to Use Google Alerts to Track Anything Automatically
claim: Alerts isn't a separate crawler — it's a saved search against Google's regular web, news, and blog index
source: Google Alerts Help Center
required_correction: Accurate general description of how Google Alerts works, consistent with Google's own documentation. No correction needed.

article_title: How to Use Google Alerts to Track Anything Automatically
claim: Clicking 'Show options' before creating an alert reveals frequency, sources, language, region, and how many results controls
source: Google Alerts Help Center — creating and managing alerts
required_correction: Matches the actual current Alerts interface options (How often, Sources, Language, Region, How many). Accurate.

article_title: How to Use Google Alerts to Track Anything Automatically
claim: Wrap exact phrases in quotes, use a minus sign to exclude a term, use OR in capitals to combine variants
source: Google Search/Alerts query operator documentation
required_correction: These are standard, documented Google search operators that carry over into Alerts query syntax. Accurate.

article_title: How to Use Google Alerts to Track Anything Automatically
claim: Google's system learns from which alert emails you open versus ignore, so consistently ignoring a noisy alert keeps it generating the same low-value results indefinitely
required_correction: No Google documentation describes Alerts as an adaptive/learning system that adjusts future results based on email open/ignore behavior — Alerts is a static saved-search-and-batch-email tool with no documented personalization-from-engagement feature. This claim should be removed or clearly flagged as speculation; it risks misleading readers into thinking ignoring emails changes future results.

article_title: How to Use Google Alerts to Track Anything Automatically
claim: Set 'How often' to at most once a day, 'Sources' to News or Blogs, and 'How many' to 'Only the best results' to cut down noise
source: Google Alerts interface (current settings and their documented effects)
required_correction: Matches current Alerts settings and their described effects; accurate practical guidance. No correction needed.

article_title: How to Use Google Alerts to Track Anything Automatically
claim: A properly filtered alert does the searching automatically, forever, for a one-time five-minute setup cost
required_correction: The article's own 'Managing Alerts' section elsewhere admits alerts need periodic review/cleanup and can silently go quiet when a source changes — this closing 'one-time cost... forever' framing contradicts that and could leave readers thinking no maintenance is ever needed. Should be reconciled with the rest of the article.

article_title: Free vs Paid Antivirus in 2026 — Do You Need to Pay
claim: Microsoft Defender consistently holds its own against paid competitors in independent testing
source: AV-TEST.org — Microsoft Defender Antivirus (Consumer) 4.18, Windows 11, May-June 2026 test; AV-Comparatives 'Is Microsoft Defender Enough?' (2026 test data)
required_correction: AV-TEST's June 2026 test scored Defender Consumer 17.5/18 (6.0 Protection, 5.5 Performance, 6.0 Usability), earning 'TOP PRODUCT' — strongly supporting the claim. However, AV-Comparatives' 2026 testing found a more mixed picture: Defender's offline detection rate (89.2%) trailed the top cluster (up to 98.6%), and it landed in the mid-range 'ADVANCED' tier (not the top 'ADVANCED+' tier) on the April 2026 Performance Test. Article should cite the actual AV-TEST score/date instead of a vague 'holds its own' claim, and note the offline-detection caveat rather than presenting Defender as unconditionally on par with paid suites.

article_title: Free vs Paid Antivirus in 2026 — Do You Need to Pay
claim: Check recent independent lab results (AV-Test, AV-Comparatives) instead of app store ratings alone — named with no actual score, date, or link cited
source: AV-TEST.org home-user Windows antivirus test results archive
required_correction: The advice to check AV-Test/AV-Comparatives is sound and both sites do publish current, checkable results (confirmed live and current as of 2026). But the article names these authorities without linking or quoting a single score — the exact 'borrowed credibility' pattern flagged editorially. Add at least one concrete recent score (e.g., AV-TEST's June 2026 scoring scale: 18 = perfect, 17.5+ = 'TOP PRODUCT' threshold) so the reference isn't just a name-drop.

article_title: Free vs Paid Antivirus in 2026 — Do You Need to Pay
claim: Android runs Google Play Protect in the background, scanning apps at install time and periodically afterward, plus the Play Store's own vetting before an app is even listed
source: Google Play Protect official documentation
required_correction: Accurate description of Play Protect's on-device app scanning at install and periodic re-scanning, plus Play Store pre-listing review. No correction needed.

article_title: Free vs Paid Antivirus in 2026 — Do You Need to Pay
claim: iOS's sandboxing model restricts what any app, malicious or not, can access, which makes a conventional scanner largely redundant on iPhone
source: Apple Platform Security documentation
required_correction: Accurate high-level characterization of iOS app sandboxing as the reason traditional file-scanning antivirus isn't offered/needed in the same way on iOS. No correction needed.

article_title: Free vs Paid Antivirus in 2026 — Do You Need to Pay
claim: Some free antivirus products have historically drawn criticism for collecting and monetizing browsing data
source: FTC enforcement action against Avast/Jumpshot over sale of browsing data collected via free antivirus/browser extensions (2024)
required_correction: This is well-documented in the general record (Avast's Jumpshot subsidiary sold browsing data collected via its free antivirus products, leading to a 2024 FTC settlement), but attempts to open the FTC press release and a corroborating news writeup both failed during this research pass (403/404 errors), so it is marked Could Not Verify per the no-fabrication rule rather than cited with an unconfirmed link. The claim as worded is vague/unnamed and technically safe, but it would be stronger editorially to name Avast/AVG specifically and cite the FTC action with a working link.

article_title: Free vs Paid Antivirus in 2026 — Do You Need to Pay
claim: Windows Security shows Defender's current status, last scan date, and whether real-time protection is active
source: Microsoft Support — Windows Security app documentation
required_correction: Accurate description of the built-in Windows Security app's functionality. No correction needed.

article_title: How to Back Up Your Phone So a Lost Device Does Not Cost You Your Photos
claim: iCloud's free storage tier is 5GB and fills up fast
source: Apple iCloud official plans page
required_correction: Accurate — Apple's free iCloud tier has remained 5GB. No correction needed.

article_title: How to Back Up Your Phone So a Lost Device Does Not Cost You Your Photos
claim: The 3-2-1 backup principle (three copies, two storage types, one off-site) scales down fine for a phone
required_correction: The 3-2-1 rule is a widely cited general data-protection principle from IT/backup practice, not a phone-specific standard or regulation, so its application to phones is sound general advice rather than a discrete checkable fact.

article_title: How to Back Up Your Phone So a Lost Device Does Not Cost You Your Photos
claim: WhatsApp chat backups are separate from phone photo backups and use their own setting, with an option to include videos
source: WhatsApp Help Center — chat backup documentation
required_correction: Accurate — WhatsApp backup settings are separate from OS-level photo backup, and the 'include videos in backup' toggle is a real, documented setting. No correction needed.

article_title: How to Back Up Your Phone So a Lost Device Does Not Cost You Your Photos
claim: Use Find My Device or Find My iPhone to lock or remotely wipe a lost phone
source: Google Find My Device and Apple Find My official support documentation
required_correction: Accurate — both services support remote lock and remote wipe. No correction needed.

article_title: How to Back Up Your Phone So a Lost Device Does Not Cost You Your Photos
claim: Standard cloud photo backups are encrypted in transit and at rest, but the provider retains access for account recovery — unlike a fully end-to-end encrypted backup, which neither Google nor Apple defaults to for photos
source: Apple Advanced Data Protection documentation
required_correction: Broadly accurate about the default state, but incomplete: Apple has offered opt-in 'Advanced Data Protection' since December 2022, which does provide end-to-end encryption for iCloud Photos if a user enables it. The article's claim that E2E is something 'neither defaults to' is correct about defaults but omits that Apple now offers a working opt-in E2E path — a meaningful, checkable detail worth adding.

article_title: How to Back Up Your Phone So a Lost Device Does Not Cost You Your Photos
claim: Moving from Android to iPhone or the reverse doesn't carry your cloud photo backup automatically between ecosystems; both companies offer a migration tool at setup time
source: Apple 'Move to iOS' app and Google cross-platform photo transfer tooling
required_correction: Accurate — Apple's 'Move to iOS' and Google's photo-transfer tools exist for cross-ecosystem migration, and neither service auto-syncs with the other by default. No correction needed.
